title: Measuring carbon mitigation potential from a network perspective: Evidence from Changsha
abstract: Promoting green travel is essential to reducing transportation-related carbon emissions, yet evidence remains limited on how to identify neighborhoods that should be prioritized for decarbonization and how to design effective policy packages. Using Changsha, China, as a case study, we integrate mobile phone data with license plate recognition data to estimate green travel demand and construct travel-related carbon emission networks to assess neighborhood-level carbon mitigation potential. We then apply an XGBoost model with SHAP analysis to examine how built-environment factors shape this potential and to design spatially differentiated policy packages. The findings reveal a clear center-periphery gradient in carbon mitigation potential. Central urban areas should be targeted with travel demand management measures, whereas peripheral areas require strengthened infrastructure. The proposed framework quantifies differences in carbon mitigation potential across urban neighborhoods and provides a basis for deploying customized low-carbon transport policies.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Tracking walking change post-relocation: A big data quasi-experiment of built environment effects
abstract: Understanding how changes in built environment (BE) affect walking behavior remains a central issue in transport research. Residential relocation offers a useful quasi-experimental setting, yet post-relocation behavioral adjustment process is largely unknown. Using year-long daily mobile-phone data from relocators in Shenzhen, this study combines Interrupted Time Series (ITS) and comparative ITS with propensity score matching to estimate both immediate and gradual effects of BE changes on walking distance. Our results reveal temporal dynamics after relocation. Higher road network density, subway density, and open space consistently promote walking, whereas land use mix shows only an initial positive effect and population density and bus stop density show only gradual effects. The study extends conventional before-and-after relocation approaches by leveraging high-frequency longitudinal data to provide a more nuanced and complete picture of BE effects. These findings highlight the importance of adopting flexible, context-sensitive and temporally informed perspectives in transport planning and policy evaluation.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Corrigendum to “Bridging socio-physical impacts, restoration efficacy and neighborhoods’ social vulnerability facing road flooding” [Transp. Res. Part D 159 (2026) 105506]
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Economic implications of EVs in Europe: A scenario analysis of value added
abstract: The transition from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric vehicles changes where value is captured in the automotive supply chain. This study introduces a vehicle-level model of passenger cars (2020–2032), linking global production data, price breakdowns, and trade flows to map gross value added across eleven value chain segments. The results show that, in 2024, the European Union captures a 12.9 percentage point lower share of gross value added from battery electric vehicles than from comparable internal combustion engine vehicles. If this gap persists in the 2032 fleet, the implied shortfall is €3,575 per vehicle. Across 2032 value chain configurations, European Union outcomes range from −€92 billion to +€63 billion relative to baseline, with local assembly and battery manufacturing as the largest levers. The study shows how the electric vehicle transition reallocates value creation across components, regions, and firm ownership, offering a granular view of Europe’s industrial and regional exposure.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Typhoon and bike-sharing: Non-linear built environment associations with activity recovery in Shenzhen
abstract: With extreme weather becoming more frequent, transportation resilience is critical. However, evidence remains limited regarding how built-environment and urban-context conditions are associated with grid-level bike-sharing activity recovery under disruption. We analyze dockless bike-sharing recovery during Typhoon Cempaka in Shenzhen using Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Generalized Additive Model (GAM), and model-based 3D response surfaces. The outcome captures service-use recovery, not individual cycling safety, welfare, or causal resilience. Results show that: (1) nighttime light intensity, population density, and distance to the nearest planned urban functional center are the leading diagnostic predictors; (2) several predictors show non-linear fitted responses, so recovery associations vary by range; and (3) the strongest interaction patterns connect activity intensity with population concentration, polycentric location, and transit accessibility. Robustness checks indicate sensitivity to baseline demand and meteorological exposure, and spatial validation shows residual spatial structure.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Financing constraints and structural drivers of maritime decarbonization
abstract: Maritime transport accounts for nearly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet decarbonization research often assumes that stronger regulation will automatically accelerate transition. This study examines how financial, technological, and regulatory conditions jointly shape the feasibility of capital mobilization in shipping. Using integrated factor extraction, perception-based causal mapping (DEMATEL), and Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA), the study identifies perceived structural interdependencies influencing maritime decarbonization finance. The results suggest that financial viability, liquidity conditions, risk-sharing mechanisms, and digital verification infrastructure are perceived as key enabling conditions, while regulatory and stakeholder factors tend to operate as reinforcing elements. Rather than indicating regulatory insufficiency, the findings highlight the interdependence between policy signals and financial-system readiness. This study contributes by integrating structural diagnostics with prioritization logic and provides policy-relevant insights for sequencing interventions in capital-intensive transport systems.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Policy pathways for low-carbon transport in Ireland: Carbon taxes and ICE bans
abstract: This paper develops I3E-Transport, a new Irish passenger transport model that integrates behavioural, technological, and macroeconomic drivers to assess the effectiveness of carbon taxation and internal combustion engine (ICE) phase-out policies on emissions from private cars and public transport. The model is soft linked to the Ireland Environment-Energy-Economy (I3E) CGE framework, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of how these policy measures influence transport demand, vehicle stock composition, energy consumption and emissions within the passenger transport sector. Simulations for 2024–2050 indicate that, under a business-as-usual scenario, emissions rise by 2050 despite modest gains in energy efficiency and alternative vehicle uptake. A carbon tax yields only limited abatement, whereas a comprehensive ICE ban from 2035—banning hybrids—reduces CO 2 emissions by over five million tonnes relative to the baseline by 2050. However, the results show that the sector remains off track relative to implied carbon budget ceilings under a 2035 implementation, with only an earlier and comprehensive ban delivering substantial progress towards compliance, pointing to the need for timely and coordinated policy action to align Ireland’s transport sector with its long-term climate commitments.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Damping-enhanced tire-pavement noise mitigation of thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber composite-modified asphalt pavements
abstract: Road traffic noise is a major environmental burden of urban transport, and tire-pavement interaction is a key source-control pathway. This study developed a damping-oriented noise-mitigation strategy for SMA-13 mixtures prepared with thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber (TPU/CR) composite-modified binders. Laboratory damping and acoustic tests were combined with a coupled tire-pavement-air finite element model incorporating explicit tread patterns to link material damping, vibration attenuation, and transition in the dominant noise source. The results showed that TPU/CR modification enhanced the critical damping ratio, with the optimum response obtained at 6 wt% TPU + 10 wt% CR, representing an increase of up to 14.46% over the CR-modified mixture. Enhanced damping promoted viscoelastic energy dissipation and reduced vibration-induced sound pressure levels. Simulations revealed a speed-dependent transition: vibration noise dominated at 60–90 km/h, whereas air-pumping noise became the main contributor above 90 km/h. TPU/CR modification therefore provides a damping-oriented source-control strategy for reducing tire-pavement noise while maintaining pavement performance.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Research on new energy vehicle diffusion via multi-subsidy trade-in policy analysis
abstract: The development of new energy vehicles (NEVs) has become one of China’s pivotal strategic initiatives for achieving low-carbon goals. Considering the renewal and further implementation of the vehicle trade-in policy in 2025, this research establishes a system dynamics model based on evolutionary game theory to analyze the market evolution of NEVs under multiple subsidy mechanisms. Through numerical simulations and sensitivity analysis, we investigate how critical model parameters influence the system, including multiple subsidies under trade-in policies, the initial strategy proportions of various stakeholders, and the composition of different consumer segments. The results demonstrate that under the current multi-subsidy mechanism, consumers ultimately show a clear trend toward participating in trade-in programs. Moreover, subsidies provided by enterprises to trade-in consumers exert a pronounced positive effect in promoting green automotive consumption. The policy recommendations proposed in this study provide clear directions for China’s NEV market amid the emerging wave of vehicle trade-in program.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Beyond connectivity: Travel behavior and hidden inequities in human mobility resilience
abstract: As climate-related extreme events intensify in frequency and severity, sustaining access to employment, healthcare, and other essential activities increasingly depends on the resilience of human mobility. This study advances mobility-resilience assessment by explicitly incorporating behavioral constraints that shape how travelers adapt under disruption. While conventional approaches largely equate resilience with transportation network connectivity, we conceptualize resilience as a behaviorally grounded outcome that depends on whether technically feasible trips remain acceptable within travelers’ limited tolerance for disruption-induced detours. Using large-scale mobile phone origin–destination data from Chongqing, China, we develop a behaviorally informed framework that integrates empirically estimated detour tolerance into resilience measurement, enabling the quantification of functional mobility loss under flood-induced network disruption. Results show that ignoring travel behavior systematically overestimates realized mobility resilience and masks critical spatial and social inequities, with low-income populations exhibiting consistently lower mobility resilience, particularly under more severe climate scenarios.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Collaborative planning framework for heavy-duty truck electrification: corridor-port integrated energy systems
abstract: Deep decarbonisation of heavy-duty truck freight is essential for global carbon neutrality. As vital intermodal hubs, ports can support the development of green freight corridors. However, existing research on port integrated energy systems primarily focuses on internal logistics and vessels, neglecting corridor- port energy-demand coupling. To bridge this gap, we propose a “Corridor-Port Integrated Energy System” (C-PIES) framework and develop a two-stage distributionally robust optimisation model to address uncertainties in renewable energy generation and freight traffic flow. Using high-frequency GPS trajectory data, ambiguity sets are constructed to support robust scheduling of port renewable energy for corridor traffic-driven loads. A case study of Quanzhou Port shows that C-PIES enables source-load-storage coordination through battery swapping stations reducing system cost by 42.89% and carbon emissions by 50.2% compared with the isolated mode. The results demonstrate the potential of ports as regional energy hubs for low-carbon freight corridors.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Route efficiency and carbon emissions of commercial UAV delivery: Evidence from Shenzhen
abstract: Urban commercial unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is increasingly regarded as a faster and potentially lower-emission alternative to ground-based logistics, yet direct evidence from repeated operations remains scarce. Using commercial telemetry from Shenzhen in 2024, this study empirically characterizes an operational UAV delivery network. We retain 45,256 valid trajectories to examine network structure and route performance. Operations are concentrated on recurrent origin-destination (OD) corridors. Compared with OSRM-routed ground alternatives between matched rounded endpoints, the mean trajectory-level route-saving ratio is 15.78%, and the mean absolute distance saving is 1.08 km per delivery. We then translate the observed route records into scenario-based operational carbon estimates. Under the baseline coefficients, estimated UAV operational emissions are 0.080 kg CO2 per delivery, compared with 0.243 kg CO2 per delivery for electric vehicle and 1.022 kg CO2 per delivery for fuel vehicle. UAV trajectories are observed, whereas ground routes and emissions are modeled under stated assumptions. The results provide an empirical basis for selective UAV deployment in urban logistics planning.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Port environmental health Risks: Insights from the Tarragona Port-Industrial complex and planning implications
abstract: Ports handle approximately 80% of world trade and concentrate vessels, cargo operations, and logistics that generate substantial pollution affecting nearby populations. Following a structured literature search and a narrative synthesis organized around a source-to-exposure-to-impact conceptual framework, this review evaluates the health risks associated with residential proximity to ports. Evidence consistently links port-related emissions to cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, asthma, lung cancer, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neurodevelopmental effects. The Tarragona Port is used as an illustrative example of a complex port-industrial setting in which port and co-located petrochemical emissions jointly contribute to a quantified local burden of preventable deaths and disability-adjusted life years, although the fraction attributable to port activities alone cannot be readily isolated from that of the adjacent petrochemical complex and other urban sources. These findings support targeted interventions, including mandatory Health Impact Assessments, health-based buffer zones, optimized freight routing, and real-time air quality monitoring integrated into port operations.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Unveiling amplified socioeconomic disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure: Accessibility versus utilization
abstract: This study examines user-centered spatial disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure by jointly analyzing accessibility (equity) and utilization (efficiency) in Shenzhen, China. It investigates how disparities differ between the two measures, and which factors explain utilization patterns. Using charging-station data, socioeconomic disparities are quantified across income and migrant groups, and a GeoXAI approach identifies nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships. Results show that disparities exist under both measures but are consistently larger during utilization. From accessibility to utilization, Gini coefficients increase by 1.1%–3.4% and Theil indices by 3.0%–9.5%. Charging stations in areas with larger low-income populations exhibit higher energy use, while those in areas with higher migrant shares are associated with longer charging durations and higher occupancy rates. Infrastructure, pricing, and built environment factors are correlated with utilization, with strong nonlinearity and spatial heterogeneity. These findings underscore utilization-aware charging evaluations and user-centered infrastructure planning.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: How do temperature and precipitation influence electric vehicle adoption? Evidence from U.S. States
abstract: Although extensive technical evidence shows that temperature and precipitation affect electric vehicle (EV) performance, less is known about how these factors translate to adoption behavior. This study examines how temperature and precipitation – incorporating both average and extreme conditions – shape EV adoption. Using panel data from 2016 to 2023 on the 48 contiguous U.S. states and the District of Columbia, we find that mean annual temperature exhibits a positive and linear relationship with EV uptake. Mean annual precipitation has no standalone effect but weakens the influence of mean temperature. Among extreme conditions, only low-temperature days (below 10°C) reduce EV adoption, while high-temperature days (above 25°C) show no significant effect. The effects of extreme precipitation are context-dependent: it promotes adoption under high-temperature conditions but shows no significant effect in cold environments. The study highlights the need for climate-sensitive and regionally tailored strategies to promote EVs and offers actionable policy recommendations.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Does public debt hinder transport decarbonization? Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence
abstract: Transport CO 2 emissions have become one of the fastest-growing sources of global greenhouse gases, posing a major challenge to sustainable development. This study examines whether, and under what conditions, public debt supports or hinders transport-sector decarbonization. We extend the debt-environment model to the transport sector, demonstrating a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions, and test it using a panel CS-ARDL approach for 31 economies from 2000 to 2021. The empirical results support a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions. Additionally, transport-related climate change mitigation technologies and environmental taxes significantly reduce emissions, suggesting their potential as effective strategies for transport decarbonization. Heterogeneity analysis reveals lower debt thresholds for low-growth and politically unstable economies. Overall, by integrating fiscal and transport sustainability within a unified theoretical framework, this study provides novel evidence and practical policy insights for designing debt-sustainable, climate-aligned transport strategies.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Electric vehicle driving range optimization considering vehicle-to-grid technology in China
abstract: Determining the optimal driving range for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) is crucial to meet user needs while minimizing production mismatch costs. The introduction of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology complicates this, as bidirectional energy flow reduces battery lifespan. This study develops a framework to determine the optimal range, considering time-of-use pricing, V2G revenues, range limitation, and battery degradation. Results show users prefer longer ranges when V2G benefits are significant. In the base case, a 400 km range meets 93.54% of user needs without considering V2G or degradation. When discharging revenue per kWh exceeds 2 times the peak-to-valley price difference, users are incentivized to choose longer ranges. Charging during shoulder periods and discharging during peak hours increases range by 4.8%; considering battery degradation, the increase is 3.4%; and when both factors are considered, the range increases by 8.8%. Waste in range, materials, and emissions is calculated based on these results.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Commute time thresholds across different city scales in urban China
abstract: Long commutes are typically considered undesirable, yet in China’s super cities, residents endure significantly longer commutes without necessarily reporting lower satisfaction. To explain this phenomenon and systematically examine the differentiated thresholds of commute satisfaction across city scales, this study adopts reference point theory and analyzes large-scale survey data from 59 Chinese cities using a two-stage machine learning approach. Results indicate that commute time is the most influential factor, with satisfaction thresholds rising alongside city scale—from 19.0 min in small cities to 43.5 min in super cities. City size moderates satisfaction in a U-shaped pattern, with a rebound in super cities linked to better transport infrastructure and social comparison effects. Thresholds also vary across commuting modes. From a behavioral economics perspective, the research clarifies the psychological mechanisms behind commute well-being, providing a scientific basis for tailored urban transport policies that enhance residents’ health and quality of life.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Social tipping in electric mobility? Lessons from the electric vehicles lead market
abstract: In most countries of the world, the diffusion of battery electric vehicles (EVs) is still limited to “innovators.” Only in Norway have EVs been so widely adopted that they have reached the “early majority” (i.e., more than 16% of the car stock). To learn what others can do to follow the front-runner, this paper reports a study of drivers and barriers of EV adoption in Norway based on a yearly, representative rolling panel survey from 2018 to 2023, interviewing more than 4000 residents per year. In Norway, the transformation to EVs was initiated by an ambitious demand-side policy. Cross-lagged panel analyses reveal that, in this context, supportive social norms were important drivers of EV adoption, amplified by self-reinforcing feedback loops, as suggested by innovation diffusion theory and research on “social tipping.” Social norms nudging may hence be a tool to accelerate the diffusion of EVs, complementing financial and infrastructure measures.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Port decarbonisation readiness of container Terminals: An Interval-Valued fuzzy TOPSIS approach
abstract: Ports are essential elements of global supply chains, yet their progress towards decarbonisation varies widely. This study develops a Port Decarbonisation Readiness Framework (PDRF) to evaluate the readiness of six container terminals in Türkiye. The framework integrates three components: entropy-based weighting of sustainability indicators, interval-valued fuzzy representation of uncertainty, and a fuzzy Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (fuzzy TOPSIS) ranking procedure. The PDRF assesses terminal-level readiness across Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions and Scope 3 mitigation readiness for onshore power supply (OPS). Because Scope 3 emissions from shipping operations are difficult to quantify, they are represented through mitigation-readiness indicators (OPS planning and electrification potential) rather than a full inventory. The results reveal substantial differences in decarbonisation readiness among terminals and demonstrate how the PDRF can support port authorities and policymakers in identifying priorities and aligning port strategies with climate goals.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Assessing the public charging serviceability for electric vehicles: an accessibility-based approach
abstract: This study proposes a serviceability assessment framework for public electric vehicle charging infrastructure (EVCI) that evaluates tract-level supply–demand gaps using charging miles per public-charging-dependent electric vehicle (EV) per day. In this framework, user exposure to reachable charging opportunities is estimated using a customized Gaussian two-step floating catchment area accessibility model that incorporates mobility-informed spatial competition. This exposure is then converted into a physically interpretable serviceability metric to provide a planning-level indicator of the estimated balance between accessible public charging service and expected charging demand. A case study in Arlington, Alexandria, and Falls Church, Virginia, USA, shows strong sensitivity to detour tolerance, with the median gap shifting from 4.54 under a 5-minute detour to − 4.45 under a 15-minute detour. Cross-scenario diagnosis indicates three decision-relevant deficit drivers: sparse supply presence in residential and suburban tracts, throughput limitations in mixed-use activity centers, and competition-sensitive coupling effects along major corridors under expanded reachability.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Noise, ferries patterns and residents’ perception: the port of Las Palmas case
abstract: Managing acoustic externalities at the port-city interface requires integrating source emissions with community perception. This study develops a framework to characterise ferry noise during hotelling, combining high-resolution monitoring with social analysis. Methodologically, AIS-synchronized measurements characterised vessel emissions, while a stratified survey evaluated resident annoyance. Results reveal L den levels of ∼67.5 dBA, exceeding industrial limits due to tonal and low-frequency penalties. These findings demonstrate that strategic maps and point measurements serve complementary purposes: the former for urban planning and the latter for designing market-based mitigation incentives to supports the ’polluter pays’ principle. Furthermore, despite low self-reported noise disturbance, hierarchical regression analysis identified residents’ health risk perception and pro-environmental behaviour as key predictors of annoyance. Specifically, the model established health risk perception as the primary factor driving heightened sensitivity. Within normalised urban noise context, concern for physical well-being acts as the principal catalyst for perceived annoyance, surpassing both ideological and contextual factors.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: When closer is not better: travel well-being among peri-urban older adults
abstract: Transportation-related subjective well-being captures emotions and satisfaction during travel and is increasingly used to evaluate the social benefits of transport and spatial policies. Using survey data from older adults in peri-urban Chengdu, China, we examine the associations of objective accessibility, perceived built-environment quality, perceived accessibility, and mobility capability with travel well-being and overall well-being. This study combines structural equation modeling, explainable machine learning, and robust interaction regressions to examine structural pathways, nonlinear patterns, and conditional associations. Perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability are positively associated with travel well-being, which is, in turn, positively associated with overall well-being. By contrast, higher objective accessibility is associated with lower travel well-being on average. This negative association tends to weaken at higher levels of perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability. The findings suggest that improvements in proximity alone may be insufficient and should be accompanied by safe, comfortable, continuous, predictable, and barrier-free walking conditions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Monitoring-based macroscopic refinement model for urban traffic noise under varying flow conditions
abstract: Urban traffic noise prediction commonly depends on traffic-based emission models, which demand extensive input data yet show limited accuracy under dynamic traffic conditions. This paper develops a noise monitoring-based macroscopic refinement model that estimates equivalent source power levels of urban traffic flow through roadside measurements. The model characterizes traffic flow as a discrete line source under free-flow conditions or a continuous one under congested flow, with source power levels derived from monitored noise and road-geometry data. Validation across four Nanjing arterials demonstrates that the model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.8–2.5 dB(A) and root mean square errors of 1.1–2.9 dB(A), showing lower errors than traffic-based approaches. An empirical reference based on flow speed ratio R for source model selection was derived from systematic performance evaluation across the tested scenarios. The framework demonstrates that roadside noise monitoring provides a practical basis for equivalent source power estimation under varying urban traffic conditions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Agent-based modelling of urban non-exhaust emissions reveals the limits of fleet electrification
abstract: As exhaust emissions decline, non-exhaust emissions (NEEs) from brake and tyre wear are emerging as the dominant source of traffic-related particulate matter. This transition is complicated by the increasing mass of electric vehicles and the push toward high-capacity public transport. We introduce a high-resolution, moving-observer agent-based model calibrated against hyperlocal Google Air View street-level measurements at the Phibsborough junction in Dublin, Ireland, a documented pollution hotspot. Global sensitivity analysis reveals that the system is fundamentally interaction-dominated: all first-order Sobol indices fall below 0.013, while total-order indices for fleet composition (0.27–0.34), mean speed (0.27), and speed variability (0.23) are substantial, confirming that traffic dynamics are as influential as fleet mix. We evaluate four policy domains informed by this sensitivity structure through passenger-preserving scenario simulation. Fleet electrification benefits are entirely contingent on regenerative braking: at 50% penetration, UFP ranges from −19% with effective regenerative braking to +13% without, while PM₂.₅ increases by 1–5% regardless of braking technology. Bus modal shift delivers the largest dual-pollutant benefits of any single intervention, peaking at 50% shift (−30% UFP, −34% PM₂.₅), though a bus paradox emerges at 75% where additional heavy buses partially offset UFP gains. Replacing ICE cars with 1,000 kg microcars yields initially modest reductions (−4% UFP at 25% adoption, rising to −30% at 75%), with diminishing returns as the unchanged SUV fleet dominates brake wear. Speed management is the most robust technology-independent lever: a 30 km/h limit reduces UFP by 16.5% and PM₂.₅ by 9% independently of fleet composition, while "slow + smooth" traffic can reduce UFP by up to 45%. A combined policy applying all five levers delivers −27% UFP and −12% PM₂.₅, demonstrating compounding benefits from coordinated action. These findings establish that speed management provides a guaranteed floor of improvement, that bus modal shift is the most effective single intervention, and that electrification must be paired with effective regenerative braking and mass-conscious vehicle choices to avoid worsening tyre-derived PM₂.₅.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Integrated traffic assignment model for evaluating shared mobility impacts on urban transportation
abstract: Shared mobility affects congestion, infrastructure, accessibility, and emissions. This paper integrates a logit choice model with a user equilibrium (UE) model to capture complexities of transportation network companies, bike sharing, and car sharing. We extend a standard UE framework by embedding shared mobility operational constraints, including fleet-size limits and rebalancing trips, enforced through a penalty function that separates the problem into two subproblems solved using the traffic assignment by paired alternative segments algorithm. We provide the first large-scale numerical analysis of integrated shared mobility impacts on the Minneapolis–St. Paul metropolitan network, which has 3061 nodes and over 9.3 million origin–destination pairs. A sensitivity analysis examines the effects of transportation network companies pricing, shared electric vehicle promotion, and micro-mobility removal on congestion, rebalancing intensity, and accessibility. Results show that minor parameter adjustments significantly influence network-wide travel behavior, traffic patterns, and emissions estimated using the motor vehicle emission simulator (MOVES).
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Total cost of ownership for CO2 carriers under alternative fuel price uncertainty
abstract: As environmental regulations become more stringent, the maritime industry faces increasing pressure to make informed decisions on alternative fuels and power systems amid substantial uncertainty in fuel costs and regulatory shifts. This study develops a techno-economic assessment framework for a CO2 carrier operating under stringent phased European Union (EU)’s environmental regulations. Economic dispatch analysis combined with Monte Carlo simulation evaluates three conventional genset systems and six alternative-fueled fuel cell (FC) systems. This study adopts the mean and the 95% value at risk (VaR95%) of the total cost of ownership (TCO) as comparative metrics. The results indicate that the blue liquid hydrogen (b-LH2) FC system achieves the lowest mean TCO and VaR95%, while the electro-methanol (e-MeOH) FC system has the highest in both metrics. Notably, VaR95% rankings differ from those based on mean TCO, underscoring the importance of risk-based evaluation. This framework supports risk-aware investment decisions for shipowners facing market volatility.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Direct and indirect impacts of road networks on vegetation cover
abstract: Road expansion balances socio-economic growth with ecological threats to vegetation cover, yet quantifying and comparing direct and indirect effects remains a challenge. This study analyzes road-vegetation dynamics (2015–2023) in Fujian, China’s first Ecological Civilization Pilot Zone, using a direct/indirect impact framework coupled with geospatial explainable artificial intelligence (Geo-XAI). Results show rising road density alongside slight vegetation recovery. Direct impact exhibits a strong negative linear correlation with road density, governed by nighttime light in cities and population density in rural areas. In contrast, indirect impact is predominantly positive, nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous, primarily governed mainly by land use intensity. Nonlinear thresholds exist nighttime light intensifies direct losses above 35 but promotes indirect gains only above 60.5; population density exacerbates direct impact up to ∼ 5,070 persons/km2, while supporting indirect benefits only below ∼ 1,270 persons/km2. The findings underscore the need for spatially targeted, pathway-specific management to harmonize infrastructure and conservation.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Editorial Board
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Private vs social costs of vehicle adoption and ownership: a sales-weighted analysis
abstract: The economic competitiveness of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) relative to internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) remains an important question for transportation and climate policy. Existing studies have largely relied on representative vehicles or scenario-based assumptions, providing limited insight into current market outcomes. This research develops a sales-weighted framework using observed sales of best-selling U.S. light-duty vehicles to evaluate both total cost of ownership and total societal cost, which incorporates carbon externalities and government purchase incentives. Results show that BEVs remain more expensive than comparable ICEVs due to higher BEV capital costs outweighing gains from lower operating costs. Monetizing carbon emissions using the societal cost of carbon reduces, but does not eliminate, the societal cost difference under 2024 market conditions. These findings suggest that economically efficient transportation electrification requires continued reduction in BEV purchase costs, electricity-sector decarbonization, and policies that more fully internalize the societal cost of carbon emissions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Public transport availability, delayed learning to drive and later life car dependence
abstract: High levels of car dependency are a major challenge for decarbonisation policy. This paper explores how early-life mobility environments shape long-run driving behaviour through two underexplored questions: whether public transport access predicts delayed learning to drive and whether the age individuals learn to drive predicts later driving intensity. We merge nationally representative survey data from Ireland ( N > 2000) with Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) scores to model (1) age at learning to drive, using survival analysis, and (2) recent driving behaviour, using a hurdle regression model. Higher public transport accessibility is associated with significantly later learning, with individuals in high‑PTAL areas 30% less likely to have learned by age 20 than those with no access. Each year of delayed learning predicts a lower likelihood of weekday driving and a 2% reduction in Vehicle Kilometres Travelled (VKT) on driving days. The findings have implications for understanding the long-term benefits of public transport provision.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: LCA-based comparisons of alternative powertrains of city buses using real-world driving cycle
abstract: The transportation sector is a major contributor to global emissions, making shifts to mass transit and low-emission powertrains essential. This study conducts a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of diesel, Battery Electric Buses (BEBs), and Hydrogen Fuel Cell Electric Buses (HFCEBs) using two approaches: Aggregate Emission-based LCA (AE-LCA), based on average fuel consumption, and Real-world Driving Cycle LCA (RDC-LCA), using GPS-derived driving cycles with second-by-second emissions estimated using CMEM and COPERT 5.6. Across all powertrains and energy pathways, RDC-LCA estimated higher Global Warming Potentials (GWPs) than AE-LCA, with deviations ranging from 8.66% for BEBs charged using captive renewable energy to 36.48% for diesel buses. HFCEBs supplied with green hydrogen achieved up to 85.50% lower GWP than diesel buses, while BEBs exhibited the lowest GWP under decarbonized electricity pathways, including renewable energy and nuclear power. These findings highlight the importance of considering vehicle powertrains and upstream energy sources to minimize transport-sector GWP.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Predicting moose (Alces alces) activity at roadside mineral licks: Implications for moose-vehicle collisions
abstract: Moose-vehicle collisions (MVCs) are a substantial cause of mortality for moose throughout some portions of their range. We investigated a series of factors that explained the timing of moose visits to roadside mineral licks (RMLs) in north-central British Columbia, Canada. Roadside mineral licks are formed by the pooling of road de-icing agents and are attractive to moose, which use them to supplement mineral intake. Moose activity was monitored with camera traps deployed at four RMLs over a 12-year period. Generalized linear mixed models suggested that snowpack and spring green-up best accounted for annual variation in the timing of spring and summer peaks of lick use by moose. Our findings can help to guide road safety planners as they develop site- and season-specific measures for mitigating MVCs which helps to increase public safety and conserve moose.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Socio-technical barriers to electric mobility in India: an expert-based integrated modelling analysis
abstract: Electric mobility is central to decarbonising transport; however, developing economies face persistent systemic barriers that limit the transition from fossil fuel-based transport. This study explores India’s case using an expert-based multi-criteria approach to map influences and hierarchical positions among 16 critical socio-technical barriers. These barriers were refined from a set of 29 barriers that were previously identified through a literature review and subsequently prioritised by domain experts. The analysis suggests that, from the perspective of experts, high purchase costs, limited domestic manufacturing capacity, and underdeveloped battery supply chains had the greatest influence on this transition, whereas charging infrastructure constraints and maintenance gaps reinforced these barriers. The cultural attachment to gasoline vehicles is perceived as a deep socio-technical constraint. The findings indicate the importance of leverage points, including cost-reduction strategies, coordinated policies to support domestic manufacturing, and accelerated deployment of charging infrastructure to support electric vehicle transition in India.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Enhancing transportation system resilience under earthquake-induced geohazards: a framework for cross-regional rescue
abstract: In mountainous areas, earthquake-induced geohazards frequently fragment road networks, isolating dispersed rural settlements and overwhelming local disaster response. Resource allocation constrained by fixed administrative boundaries often fails to adapt to the connectivity of road networks. We propose a coupled simulation framework that integrates an agent-based model with network science to strengthen the resilience of transportation systems in response to earthquake-induced geohazards. This framework simulates cascading failures in transportation system functionality that affect human mobility, enabling the assessment of how physical disruptions constrain organizational decision-making. Sensitivity and robustness analyses addressing macrolevel environmental constraints, microlevel behavioral attributes, and conditions under cross-factor scenarios revealed that this approach substantially enhances system resilience, particularly under high disaster intensity and limited resources. This study shows that improving transportation system functionality during disasters requires aligning emergency management strategies with the topological realities of networked mobility.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Tracking sustainability dynamics in EU transport sector: Bayesian latent change-score analysis study
abstract: This study examines the structural drivers of greenhouse gas emissions in the European Union’s transport sector by integrating freight activity and logistics performance within a Bayesian Latent Change Score framework. This approach, rarely applied in transport-emissions research, captures dynamic feedback, measurement error, and period-specific effects across three policy intervals (2007–2012, 2012–2018, and 2018–2023). Results show a stable and positive effect of freight activity on emissions, indicating persistent structural inertia in the sector. In contrast, the influence of logistics performance is time-varying, becoming increasingly negative as EU environmental regulation strengthens. This suggests that logistics efficiency contributes to decarbonization only once supportive governance and market conditions are in place. By combining longitudinal EU-27 data with an advanced dynamic modeling strategy, the study provides novel empirical evidence on how logistics systems and policy environments jointly shape transport-sector emission trajectories and informs long-term decarbonization strategies.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Passenger-freight shared mobility for decarbonizing urban-rural bus systems: fleet and capacity optimization
abstract: Urban-rural public transport faces a self-reinforcing cycle of declining ridership, service deterioration, and mounting deficits, while parallel diesel freight operations generate substantial carbon emissions along the same corridors. Passenger-freight shared mobility (PFSM) addresses both challenges by using idle bus capacity to co-transport parcels, yet its implementation must balance passenger service quality and freight efficiency. This study formulates a bilevel optimization model that jointly determines fleet composition, and dynamic capacity allocation, and vehicle scheduling while incorporating stochastic travel time effects of freight operations. An improved jellyfish search algorithm is developed to solve the resulting mixed-integer program. A case study of two urban–rural routes in Shanxi Province, China, shows that the optimized PFSM scheme turns a daily operating deficit of RMB 2462.16 into a profit of RMB 537.55, eliminates dedicated freight trucks, and reduces annual freight-related CO2 emissions by 19.12 tons per route, demonstrating a viable pathway for decarbonizing rural transport.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Real-world battery electric vehicle charging and driving behavior estimation and quantification
abstract: Newer, longer-range electric vehicles (EVs) drive approximately 12,000 miles annually, approaching the 14,000-mile annual average for gas vehicles, highlighting the importance to understand better EV charging and driving behavior as EVs become mainstream. Using U.S. EV driving, parking, and charging data from 2018 to 2019 and 2023–2024, we analyzed how drivers use charging infrastructure and predicted charging likelihood. A random-forest model was used to screen for key factors, informing an interpretable mixed logit model with about 80 % out-of-sample accuracy. Drivers of longer-range EVs in 2023–2024 primarily charged at home, but plugged in roughly 25 % less often at home at the end of the day than drivers of shorter-range EVs when state of charge was 50 %. Charging was more likely (∼5–9 %) in the Northeast than in other regions, particularly in winter. Additionally, greater public charging availability may also be associated with an increase in the probability of away-from-home charging.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Ports in transition: rethinking hydrogen hub site selection through a multi-stakeholder lens
abstract: Green hydrogen is central to decarbonizing energy and transport systems, with ports increasingly positioned as key locations for hydrogen-related activities. However, the specific functions of ports within emerging hydrogen value chains and the evolving multi-stakeholder dynamics surrounding their development remain underexplored. The objective of this study is to develop a conceptual multi-actor multi-criteria decision-making framework for hydrogen hub site selection in ports. Drawing on a narrative literature review and expert interviews, we identify four distinct functions in the hydrogen value chain: industrial hydrogen hubs, bunkering-oriented hubs, import–export gateways, and distribution and aggregation nodes. Each function involves specific infrastructure requirements, stakeholder constellations, and decision criteria. By incorporating stakeholder salience and function-specific objectives into the decision logic, our framework structures early-stage decision-making around divergent interests and governance complexity. We contribute to the port development and infrastructure planning literature by introducing hydrogen-related port functions, conceptualizing their evolution, and integrating multi-stakeholder governance into decision-making.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Decarbonizing the maritime sector: cold ironing and e-fuels. Case study: Gran Canaria
abstract: This research addresses the decarbonization of the maritime transport considering the services that can be provided at port, by analyzing both cold ironing and e-fuels production. To this end, the electricity demand for both processes is estimated, as well as the resulting electricity generation cost and the associated emissions, enabling an estimate of the climate neutrality cost. Two possible scenarios were considered for the renewable e-fuel production: dedicated renewable farms versus renewable surpluses coming from the island electricity system. For the cold ironing different scenarios are being considered: electricity coming from the grid and renewable farms to produce the required electricity. The island of Gran Canaria (Canary Islands, Spain) is considered as the case study. The results show a potential reduction of 483 kt of CO 2 -eq (9) % of the island’s emissions) and a levelized cost of energy ranging from 181 to 616 €/MWh, depending on the scenario and e-fuel considered.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Equity by design in electric vehicle charging infrastructure networks
abstract: Public charging infrastructure extends electrified miles, reduces range anxiety, and promotes electric vehicle adoption. However, charging stations remain inaccessible to underserved and disadvantaged populations. To address this, we propose a novel location model for equitable electric vehicle charging infrastructure placement, with objectives to minimize detours for charging and improve trip completion for low-income travelers and multi-unit dwelling residents, who face shorter electric vehicle ranges and limited home charging access. A genetic algorithm-based approach with column generation is used to solve the multi-objective nonlinear bilevel programming problem and identify Pareto-optimal solutions. The proposed method is applied to the state of Illinois transportation network as a case study. We assume universal electric vehicle adoption to represent a forward-looking public planning scenario, rather than calibrating infrastructure solely to current ownership patterns that reflect existing socioeconomic disparities. The results show that our equity-by-design siting improves accessibility for disadvantaged travelers while maintaining service quality and performance for all privileged users. Through analysis of various scenarios, we offer insights into the robustness of equitable charging station placement. Our analysis indicates that (i) siting meeting only cost efficiency priorities can coincide with equitable outcomes but represents only a subset of Pareto-optimal solutions, whereas planning charging location driven by equity reveals various alternatives; (ii) the fewer the charging stations, the more missed trips that leave lower-income and multi-unit dwelling residents and travelers the most vulnerable; (iii) in the early stages of transportation electrification, when charging infrastructure is sparser, it is likely that disparities in charging access will be observed among socioeconomic groups but as the charging network grows denser these accessibility gaps will be bridged.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: A framework for sustainable robotaxi infrastructure in emerging cities
abstract: This study proposes an integrated planning framework for robotaxi deployment in medium-sized cities by combining MCDM, GIS-based spatial analysis, and robustness assessment. Intended primarily for local governments and urban transport authorities, the framework also provides operators and investors with an analytical baseline for fleet sizing and charging-infrastructure planning. Seven main criteria and 32 sub-criteria were weighted using FWZIC and RANCOM, with strong agreement confirmed by Pearson correlation (r = 0.9620), Spearman correlation (ρ = 0.9643), and MAD (0.00728). A normalized [0–1] suitability map was used to delineate feasible service areas. The baseline scenario assumes 200 robotaxis, including 150 active and 50 standby vehicles, with rem-based allocation for staging. Using Tesla Model Y Juniper data as a proxy, total grid-side fleet energy demand was estimated at 9.96 MWh/day. Peak-period sizing indicates that at least nine DC fast-charging units are required for the daytime DC charging component.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Investigating and comparing user experiences at EV charging and petroleum fueling stations
abstract: Light duty electrification requires DC charging stations to take over the current role of petroleum stations. However, charging and fueling systems differ substantially in technology, user behavior, and business models. This study analyzes thousands of reviews for petroleum stations and DC charging stations. Using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative rating, sentiment analysis, and Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted topical classification, factors that shape user experience are identified. Charging and fueling are perceived as fundamentally different activities. Fueling reviews are dominated by fuel price and staff interaction, while charging reviews emphasize equipment reliability, location convenience, and access to nearby amenities. Manufacturer-owned charging networks are perceived more positively than open networks. Open networks suffer from small station sizes and higher outage rates which reduce effective capacity and generate negative feedback. Across networks, proximity to amenities strongly influences perceived convenience and satisfaction. These findings identify actionable pathways for improving charging experiences and perceptions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Bus fleet electrification: A comprehensive review of charging, operations, planning and sustainability
abstract: Battery Electric Buses (BEBs) are increasingly adopted by Local PublicTransit (LPT) companies as a strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissionsand support sustainable mobility transitions. However, BEB deployment in-troduces new challenges related to charging infrastructures, operational con-straints, investment decisions and long-term planning. This paper presentsan up-to-date review of more than 100 studies published between 2019 and2025 on bus fleet electrification. The analysis identifies four major researchdirections Charging Infrastructure and Methods, Bus Fleet Operations, Elec-trification Planning, and Sustainability, highlighting their interdependenciesand methodological trends. Across these works, several recurring themesemerge, including the central role of optimized charging strategies on totalcost of ownership, the increasing coupling between fleet scheduling and en-ergy management, and the need for integrated planning models that jointlyconsider infrastructure, battery sizing, and operations. The review also re-veals persistent gaps related to uncertainty modeling, scalability for largetransport networks, and careful consideration of battery degradation. Fi-nally, a functional framework is proposed to synthesize how current researchcontributions map onto the practical decision layers faced by LPT operators.This work provides a consolidated foundation for future studies and supportspractitioners in navigating the complexities of large-scale BEB deployment.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Getting there and feeling better: mechanisms from perceived accessibility to subjective well-being
abstract: Accessibility matters for subjective well-being, yet its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Using survey data from 5591 respondents in ten Chinese cities, this study examines how perceived accessibility relates to hedonic and eudaimonic well-being through domain-specific travel satisfaction and social exclusion. After accounting for the indirect pathways, the structural equation modeling results show that perceived accessibility remains positively associated with flourishing and negatively associated with negative affect, whereas its total effect on positive affect is not significant. The mediation effect varies across travel domains and well-being outcomes. Leisure travel satisfaction emerged as the most important mediator for flourishing, while shopping travel satisfaction played a mediation role across all outcomes. Commute travel satisfaction was particularly salient for affective well-being. Social exclusion, meanwhile, constituted a strong and consistent pathway. The findings highlight that accessibility contributes to well-being not only through reaching destinations, but also through satisfying travel experiences and social inclusion.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: A multi-criteria readiness assessment of cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle infrastructure
abstract: This study develops an integrated decision-support framework for assessing the readiness of major Turkish cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle (AV) infrastructure. İstanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Bursa, and Antalya are evaluated using 16 sub-criteria grouped under Physical Infrastructure, Smart Mobility, Sustainability, and Adaptive Capacity. Expert judgments are consolidated through the Modified Delphi method and analyzed using Pythagorean Fuzzy Indifference Threshold-based Attribute Ratio Analysis (PF-ITARA) and Pythagorean Fuzzy Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (PF-MARCOS). The results identify Economic Feasibility, Municipal Capacity, and R&D Ecosystem as the most influential criteria. İzmir ranks first, followed by İstanbul, Ankara, Bursa, and Antalya. Sensitivity analyses confirm that İzmir remains the leading city under alternative threshold structures and 32 criterion-weight perturbation scenarios. The findings show that autonomous vehicle readiness depends on balanced technological, financial, institutional, and sustainability capabilities and provide practical guidance for urban infrastructure planning and phased deployment.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Enhancing sustainability and cost-efficiency in urban rail-road bridge: A Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted framework
abstract: Cities increasingly require sustainable and land-efficient transportation infrastructure. While Integrated Rail-Road Bridge (IRRB) optimizes urban land use by combining rail and road into a single bridge, integration alone is insufficient to minimize environmental and economic burdens. Consequently, as horizontal alignment is the primary determinant of economic and environmental footprints, optimizing horizontal geometry is imperative for developing land-efficient and sustainable urban corridors. To address this, we propose a Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted Multi-Objective Horizontal Curve Optimization (MOHCO) framework. It comprises a data-driven phase for initial impact datasets, a Bayesian-optimized surrogate model for rapid, high-fidelity impact predictions across high-dimensional design spaces, and a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) multi-objective optimization incorporating CO2 emissions and contribution to local temperature. Applied to a real-world case, the framework achieved high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.98), reduced cost by 5.64%, environmental impact by 38.90%, and improved safety by 44.40% compared to manual designs, supporting sustainable urban transportation development.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Impacts of speed limits on emissions, energy consumption and traffic efficiency
abstract: A field experiment is conducted to investigate operational benefits of speed-limit control in platooning traffic, where the leading vehicle travels at a constant cruise speed while an additional speed-limit control is imposed on following vehicles. First, the effects of speed limits on traffic oscillation dynamics and traffic flow performance are analyzed. Results indicate that restricting the maximum speed of vehicles can stabilize traffic flow, reduce oscillation frequency, and lower emissions and energy consumption (EEC), but may reduce traffic throughput due to an increase in platoon length. A simulation framework is then developed to extend this investigation to broader speed levels and bottleneck scenarios. The results show that speed-limit control should vary with cruising speed to balance EEC and traffic efficiency, and that the proposed solutions apply to traffic management strategies. These findings enrich our understanding of traffic dynamics under speed-limit control strategies and provide practical insights for their real-world implementation.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Development of regional heavy-duty vehicle driving cycles based on optimized Markova chain
abstract: Driving cycles are essential for vehicle energy and emission standards, but standard cycles often overlook regional variations. This study proposes a novel framework for constructing representative driving cycles for heavy-duty vehicles by optimizing a Markov chain with a hybrid Multi-Population Genetic Algorithm and Wavelet Threshold Denoising (hMPGA-WTD). The methodology involves: (1) spectral clustering of 1.27 million telematics data points to identify operational scenarios; (2) generating scenario-specific cycles using a two-dimensional Markov chain; and (3) enhancing driving cycle fidelity with hMPGA-WTD to reduce feature distortions. The method achieves a mean relative error of 4.61% across key parameters, with velocity standard deviation error below 1%. It outperforms micro-trip concatenation and conventional Markov approaches. Fuel consumption is validated via real-world and chassis dynamometer tests under identical loads, showing a 4.26% deviation, better than the 7.71% under CHTC-TT. The framework offers a robust basis for efficiency assessment and standard development.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Slow and steady wins the race: How autonomy facilitates long-haul truck electrification
abstract: This paper examines how autonomy affects the competitiveness and operations of battery-electric long-haul trucks. We model fleet operations between Sydney and Melbourne—Australia’s busiest long-haul corridor—using a parameterised cost-minimisation framework. By lowering travel-time costs, autonomy leads to slower optimal speeds and reduced energy use. This enables smaller, lighter battery packs or reduces the number of charging stops en route, lowering total costs. Autonomy thus enhances the economic case for battery-electric trucks, improving their cost competitiveness relative to diesel trucks commensurate with an AUS$34/kWh reduction in battery pack price (ranging from about AUS$10 to AUS$75/kWh across sensitivities).
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Drive or breathe? Information-aware mode choice under real-time exposure using ICLV-CMXL approach
abstract: Commuters in urban areas face prolonged exposure to air pollution. This study assessed whether providing commuters with real-time, trip-specific air pollution information can encourage a shift towards public transit modes. Sequential integrated choice and latent variable model with a correlated mixed logit component is developed using stated choice data and user perceptions for motorized transport users in Delhi. Real-time pollution information for current modes was obtained through a multimodal router. Perceptions included air quality awareness, availability and usability of air quality information, and willingness to change behavior for primary trips. The results indicate that people with a better understanding of air quality information and its usage are inclined to choose public transit. Motorized two-wheeler users are more sensitive to exposure compared to car users, showing a stronger preference for public transit. These findings highlight the importance of real-time information in mode shift. Policymakers can formulate strategies to reduce individuals’ exposure in public transit.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Carbon-efficient ride-pooling at intercity railway hubs: Nonlinear topological mechanisms and algorithmic insights
abstract: Ride-pooling (RP) can reduce transport emissions, but its carbon reduction potential across spatial contexts remains unclear, especially at intercity transfer hubs. Using citywide regulatory ride-hailing data from Suzhou, China, this study examines how meso-level path topology features are associated with carbon reductions in railway station pooling. Railway station pooled trips show 62.6% higher carbon reductions per trip than the overall pooled-trip sample average, influenced by nonlinear mechanisms and interaction patterns rather than higher pooling intensity. An explainable machine learning framework shows that carbon efficiency is primarily associated with route quality, as reflected in path topology, operational scenarios, and built environment factors. In particular, detour constraints, common drop-off configurations, and their interactions with distance act as critical thresholds. Building on these insights, we develop a dual-layer classification framework that can identify pooling matches with high carbon reduction potential prior to dispatch (accuracy ≥ 96%). These findings suggest that intercity railway stations may serve as favorable contexts for low-carbon RP when demand concentration and route quality align. This insight can help guide matching strategies that are enabled by AI and informed by carbon efficient in shared mobility systems.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Promoting energy transition in shipping: An evolutionary game analysis of green corridors
abstract: Green corridors are emerging as a practical mechanism to promote alternative fuels. This paper develops an evolutionary game model to better understand the interactions between shipping lines and cargo owners within a green corridor. A population of 15,000 TEU container ships traveling between Australia and Singapore is simulated to study the economic feasibility of three alternative fuels: liquefied natural gas (LNG), methanol, and ammonia. The results indicate that LNG and methanol have a competitive advantage, while ammonia appears less economically attractive under the assumptions and parameter settings adopted in this study, primarily because of its higher associated costs. Sensitivity analysis reveals cargo owners’ willingness to pay (WTP) for alternative fuels, port discounts, and carbon tax significantly influence the fuel transition. It confirms the shipping industry is likely to be particularly sensitive to the cargo owners’ preference for alternative fuels. The study also highlights the importance of coordination among key stakeholders.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Robust low-carbon ship routing under weather uncertainty: a distributional reinforcement learning approach
abstract: Maritime transport carries most global trade yet contributes roughly 3% of greenhouse-gas emissions, and as the IMO targets a 20–30% reduction by 2030 and the EU prices maritime carbon, deterministic routing is increasingly inadequate. This study merges distributional reinforcement learning with distributionally robust optimization for low-carbon routing under spatial weather uncertainty. A quantile-regression deep Q-network (QR-DQN) captures stochastic weather impacts, a Wasserstein-metric DRO term addresses train–deployment distribution shift, and a physics-informed reward embeds hydrodynamic resistance and carbon-intensity compliance. On the Rotterdam–New York corridor, the framework cuts fuel use by 17.9% versus slow steaming and 5.1% versus a standard DQN (about 390 tonnes of CO2 per voyage, with direct EU ETS and CII relevance), while keeping adverse-weather exposure near zero and fuel variability low. Ablations attribute this consistency mainly to the physics-informed reward, with the critic securing stable training and efficiency and the robust layer curbing tail degradation under shift.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Impact of environmental functions on electric vehicle charging experience considering contextual constraints
abstract: As the electric vehicle market expands, improving public charging experience has become critical to the sustainability of urban transport. Using Wuhan as an empirical case, this study develops a double machine learning framework to examine how urban functional environments shape charging experience through charging behavior, while incorporating competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation as contextual constraints. Based on tens of millions of charging records, three main findings emerge. First, the functional environment has a significant positive causal effect on charging experience, about 60% of which is mediated by charging behavior. Second, only a few behavior types generate disproportionate experience gains, and these behaviors are linked to the joint presence of particular nearby urban functions. Third, moderate levels of competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation amplify both the total effect and behavioral mediation. These findings inform station siting, operational optimization, and charging-network planning.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: An evaluation method for the fume emission intensity of rubber-modified asphalt binders
abstract: Accurately quantifying fume emission intensity from rubber-modified asphalt binders is essential for sustainable construction and air-pollution mitigation. This study proposes an evaluation method based on maximum emission rate, peak concentration, and total emission amount. Feasibility was verified through variability, sensitivity, and comparative analyses. The method was applied to rubber-modified asphalt binders at different activation temperatures and multi-source aging durations to quantify fume emission intensity. Microscopic mechanisms were analyzed using fluorescence microscopy (FM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Results indicate good reliability, with parallel experimental variability of 4.94% and a deviation within ±0.03 in weighted sensitivity analysis. Microscopic observations corroborated the macroscopic emission trends: high-temperature activation damaged the rubber structure and increased its solubility, more than doubling fume emission intensity, whereas multi-source aging reduced light components and decreased emissions by approximately 20%.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment of urban road network system under unexpected subway failures
abstract: The unexpected subway failures cause numerous passengers to gather, exerting pressure on the urban road network system (URNS) through their complementary relationship. This study proposes a dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment framework for the URNS under the unexpected subway failures, encompassing both internal functionality and external environment. First, the dependence between subway stations and road intersections is established to quantify transferred passenger flows. Second, a load-capacity model is developed, which treats the surge in origin–destination traffic demand as the triggering condition for cascading effect. Finally, by correlating the functional degradation of the URNS with the resulting increase in carbon emissions, dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment metrics are proposed. A case study of Futian District, Shenzhen, indicates that subway line criticality differs across dimensions. The findings provide a decision-making basis for enhancing the resilience of subway–road transport systems while balancing operational functionality and environmental impacts.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Understanding the heterogeneity of willingness to share: Ridesplitting’s adoption and usage frequency
abstract: Ridesplitting, a shared urban mobility service, is widely regarded as a promising way to alleviate the negative impacts of ride-hailing, yet its market penetration remains low. Existing studies provide limited understanding of spatiotemporal and user heterogeneity in willingness to share (WTS). To fill this gap, we conduct a questionnaire survey in Beijing and apply latent class analysis to identify user segments based on psychological factors related to ridesplitting. Binary logit model and scenario analysis are then used to examine sharing behavior and mode conversion across segments. Results show that both ridesplitting and non-ridesplitting users exhibit substantial heterogeneity in WTS. Moderately satisfied users show strong potential for more frequent use, while improving travel time reliability and cost savings can convert likely adopters into active participants. These findings inform policies and platform strategies to promote sustainable urban mobility.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Corrigendum to “Public or private? A unified demand–supply coupled framework for EV infrastructure investment” [Trans. Res. Part D: Trans. Environ. 159 (2026) 105501]
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Wildfire shrinks shelter access unevenly across California
abstract: This study advances disaster decision-making by embedding wildfire expected annual loss (EAL) into cumulative shelter access measurements across California. Departing from conventional metrics that assume full facility availability during wildfire events, it applies an EAL-weighted adjustment across multiple travel-time thresholds. Three findings emerge from the multi-scalar analysis at the census block group and county levels. First, EAL weighting consistently reduces shelter access and reveals geographically uneven proportional losses within counties. Second, county-level disparities are most persistent where extensive wildland–urban interface (WUI) development, uneven shelter distribution, concentrated wildfire exposure, and limited transportation networks coincide. Longer travel-time thresholds reduce within-county disparities in many counties yet do not eliminate structural access constraints in WUI-dominated counties. Third, although EAL-weighted access does not reveal systematic racial disparities, inequities persist by income and vehicle ownership. The framework supports mitigation-oriented identification of structurally vulnerable communities before wildfire occurrence and informs risk-aware resource allocation.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Unraveling divergence in pavement LCA tools through attribution analysis
abstract: Specialized life cycle assessment (LCA) tools are increasingly used for pavement sustainability assessment, yet they can yield divergent results for the same project. This study compares five representative tools—MIT Streamlined Pavement LCA & LCCA Tool, LCA Pave, HERMES CO2, Athena Pavement LCA, and asPECT—using four harmonized pavement cases for a 1 km × 3.5 m lane over 50-year period. For embodied/infrastructure-related GHG emissions, project-level tools gave comparable estimates; for the asphalt freeway case, MIT, LCA Pave, and Athena ranged from 364 to 435 t CO2-eq/lane-km. When operational emissions were included, PVI-related use-stage effects accounted for 71 %-89 % of full life-cycle GHG in MIT and Athena. Attribution analysis shows that divergence mainly arises from system boundary, LCIA method, traffic-fuel baseline, roughness-fuel modelling, albedo treatment, and recycling-credit assumptions. Tool disagreement should therefore be interpreted modularly by life-cycle stage to guide future improvement.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Sustainable transport in the climate-change era
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Explaining temporal and spatial variability in shared e-scooter ridership in Christchurch, New Zealand
abstract: Shared electric scooters (e-scooters) are widely adopted, yet their ridership patterns remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies rely on origin-destination (OD) inferred trips and use global models, which overlook true paths and spatial heterogeneity effects. This constrains understanding of spatio-temporal patterns and drivers of shared e-scooter ridership, reducing the effectiveness of transport planning and policy interventions. We address these limitations using observed street-segment-level trip counts to identify spatio-temporal ridership profile by clustering hourly ridership curves. We also apply Geographically Weighted Poisson Regression (GWPR) to examine spatial associations between ridership and contextual factors. Results reveal clear temporal differences from cycling behaviour and strong spatially varying associations between ridership and built environment, which global models fail to capture. Our findings show that data-driven clustering can classify micromobility behaviour without assuming trip purpose.
