Although focused on Christchurch, the methodological framework is transferable and applicable to other cities with similar data.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Integrated AHP–Entropy–Game Theory and GIS framework for EV charging station site selection
abstract: The rapid growth of electric mobility requires robust frameworks for optimal electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) deployment. This study proposes an integrated spatial decision-support framework combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Entropy Weight Method (EWM), game-theoretic deviation-minimization weighting, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to identify suitable EVCS locations in İzmir, Türkiye. The approach integrates literature-informed AHP-based prioritization with entropy-derived analytical weighting for balanced multi-criteria spatial analysis. Results show that proximity to electricity transmission lines receives the highest weight and should be interpreted as an infrastructure-proximity and potential grid-connection feasibility proxy, rather than a direct measure of grid capacity or electricity-system adequacy. Population density and major accessibility factors, including main roads and transport stations, contribute to suitability as indirect demand and mobility proxies. Highly suitable zones are mainly concentrated in central and northern districts (Konak, Karşıyaka, Bornova, Bayraklı), covering 6.51 % of the area, while 17.08 % is classified as suitable.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Understanding e-cargo bike substitution of car, cycling, and walking through domestic trials in three UK cities
abstract: This study examines ECB mode substitution using a mixed-methods approach combining travel diaries from 42 households participating in real-world ECB trials across Leeds, Oxford, and Brighton with 111 interviews. ECB trips mostly replaced car travel (60%), followed by conventional cycling (23%) and walking (17%). Regression analysis showed that car substitution was more likely among men, older adults, retirees, multi-car households and for passenger-carrying, shopping, child-escorting, and leisure trips. Qualitative findings further described a gradual process of building confidence, adapting routines, and integrating the ECB into everyday mobility, enabling progressively greater car substitution. For some, the ECB was viewed as a realistic alternative to a second car. The findings show that ECBs offer a versatile family mobility solution with substantial sustainability potential by reducing vehicle mileage and emissions, while supporting transitions towards car ownership renunciation. The study details targeted policy interventions that can maximise ECBs uptake and their contribution to sustainability.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Managing autonomous vehicle accessibility to mitigate environmental rebound effects
abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) services can improve urban mobility, but excessive door-to-door convenience may shift users from public transport and increase zero-occupant vehicle (ZOV) circulation. This study treats AV access time as a policy-controllable variable and evaluates its environmental and operational effects under fixed peak-hour demand. An integrated framework combines synthetic demand preprocessing, multi-modal user equilibrium assignment, explicit ZOV loading, and reinforcement-learning policy search. Results show that reducing access time below about five minutes sharply increases empty vehicle movements, total system travel time, and CO2 emissions. Within a restricted generic road-charging framework, a six-minute access time with a moderate per-trip charge forms a constrained Pareto-knee. Extending the policy space to ZOV-targeted instruments, including empty-VKT charges, reduces reliance on generic road charges and improves network performance, reducing CO2 emissions by up to 15.0% relative to the fixed reference condition (Base=100) while preserving public transport shares.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Editorial Board
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: An integrated simulation and optimization framework for mixed-fleet public transit decarbonization
abstract: Public transit agencies face growing pressure to decarbonize operations while maintaining reliable service. Planning and operating mixed fleets of diesel, battery-electric, and hydrogen buses requires modelling tools that capture interactions among vehicle energy use, charging and refueling infrastructure, and network operations. This paper presents MLTransit, an integrated simulation-optimization framework that links general transit feed specification preprocessing, agent-based operational modelling, and multi-stage optimization to evaluate transit decarbonization strategies under realistic service patterns. The framework represents vehicle energy consumption, nonlinear charging behavior, queueing at charging facilities, battery degradation, emissions, and grid constraints. A two-stage optimization assigns service blocks to feasible vehicle types and determines cost-efficient charging infrastructure and policy parameters, while detailed charging schedules emerge endogenously through simulation. Applied to the Metro Vancouver bus network, MLTransit evaluates trade-offs between depot-only and combined depot-opportunity charging, showing that combined charging improves operational feasibility and service reliability at the cost of higher infrastructure investment.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Emission reduction potential of freeway stop-and-go wave smoothing
abstract: The real-world potential of stop-and-go wave smoothing at scale remains largely unquantified. Smoothing freeway waves requires opening a gap large enough for them to dissipate, but that gap is often impractically large. We propose a counterfactual wave-smoothing benchmark that reconstructs a smooth, feasible trajectory from each empirical trajectory by solving a quadratic program with fixed boundary conditions and a maximum-gap constraint, and we use the MOVES model to estimate the resulting emission reduction potential. Applying the framework to nine weeks of weekday peak-period data from the I-24 MOTION testbed, which exhibits rich day-to-day variation in wave dynamics, we find meaningful potential for passenger cars under a 0.1-mile maximum-gap constraint: average CO 2 reductions of 9.80% to 14.08% across lanes, with 12.94% to 25.70% in CO, 24.29% to 29.76% in HC, and 29.40% to 36.03% in NOx. Trucks emerge as particularly attractive targets, showing roughly twice the reduction potential of passenger cars.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: How does harassment alter cycling satisfaction? Insights from London
abstract: Cycling satisfaction is a key factor in increasing cycling mode share, particularly in low-cycling contexts such as England. Satisfaction is subjective and shaped by both observable conditions and unobserved psychological factors. One important but understudied factor is harassment, which can take many forms (e.g., verbal, physical, sexual, racial, or identity-based) and may strongly influence cyclists’ experiences. This study develops a quantitative framework to examine how harassment affects cycling satisfaction through a latent variable representing harassment-related experiences, using survey data from 1,525 cyclists in London. Results show that cyclists who feel stressed, unsafe, or threatened are significantly more likely to report dissatisfaction, even after controlling for socio-demographic factors. Harassment-related perceptions are strongly associated with traffic exposure, lighting conditions, and accumulated near-miss or collision experiences. These findings demonstrate that cycling satisfaction is significantly associated with harassment-related perceptions and highlight the need to incorporate harassment-sensitive measures into cycling level-of-service evaluations.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Contextualising the impact of street slopes on pedestrian accessibility for sustainable mobility
abstract: Proximity-based planning has become a central paradigm in transport policy, guiding the design of sustainable, accessible, and liveable cities. This shift has driven the development of various methods for assessing pedestrian accessibility, reflecting the central role of walking as the most sustainable mode. Yet, the impact of street slopes on accessibility is often neglected and remains poorly understood. This study identifies two systematic biases: a slope-speed bias, caused by assuming flat terrain, and a slope-preference bias, reflecting behavioural aversion to slopes. We compare three models: (a) slope-agnostic, (b) slope-adjusted with gradient-dependent speeds, and (c) slope-preference incorporating walking preferences across walking propensity groups. Applied in Athens, Greece, results show that slope-agnostic models overestimate accessibility by approximately 6–8% on average. Accounting for walking preferences introduces an additional 33–40% reduction for low-propensity walkers across destination types. The proposed framework offers a transferable approach for integrating terrain sensitivity into accessibility analysis.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Do aviation hazard rankings overlook conservation-concern birds in U.S. wildlife strikes?
abstract: Airports concentrate aircraft and birds in shared space, making wildlife strikes a flight-safety problem and a documented source of avian mortality. We analyze 343,997 U.S. wildlife-strike records from 1990 to 2025 with a framework that corrects for reporting growth, models per-strike severity, and ranks species by aviation hazard and conservation status. A detection-aware count model bounds the true rise in the strike rate between 3.4 and 8 fold, below the widely cited fourteen-fold rise in the reported rate. A random-parameters ordered probit shows that engine ingestion and body mass dominate severity, with the mass effect growing more variable at higher impact speeds. Conservation weighting shifts 112 of 310 ranked species by more than 30 places, elevating aerial insectivores, migratory warblers, and grassland passerines, including the Vulnerable Chimney Swift. The results support region- and season-specific mitigation that protects aircraft and declining birds together.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Challenges in comparing measured and modelled annual average noise levels around airports
abstract: Aircraft noise has a significant impact on communities near airports. To regulate noise, annual average levels such as L den are modelled across large areas. This study examines the consistency between L den predicted by the European Civil Aviation Conference Doc 29 model and measurements from noise monitoring terminals around Amsterdam Airport Schiphol from 2017 to 2024. While strong correlations confirm Doc29′s suitability for system-level assessments, systematic biases persist, with nighttime levels L night generally overestimated and L den underestimated. Three potential sources were identified: difference between modelled and flown tracks, background noise influencing measured levels, and undetected flights, particularly for quieter aircraft and in low noise regions. Accounting for these factors improves correlation and reduces deviation between measurements and predictions. These results demonstrate promising methods for enabling noise model validation near airports. Further improvements in detection methods and operational modelling will increase the robustness of noise assessments and better support evidence-based policy development around major airports.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Pragmatism, not ideology: drivers of e-bike sharing usage intensity
abstract: What drives usage intensity among registered e-bike sharing system (EBSS) users – distinguishing power users from dormant registrants – remains underexplored despite its importance for system viability. We link survey responses from 1,844 registered users to their individual trip histories within an operational dataset of 1.4 million trips from free-floating S-Pedelec and dock-based e-bike sharing systems operating concurrently in Basel, Switzerland. Using Gaussian Mixture Model clustering and an ordered logit model, we find that usage is highly concentrated (Gini = 0.77) and primarily substitutes public transport. Pro-environmental self-identity negatively associates with high-intensity user (“power-user”) status. Instead, intensive use is associated with multimodal integration and perceived functional superiority over public transport. System design distinguishes two distinct pragmatic archetypes: dock-based “routine optimizers” and free-floating “flexibility maximizers”. These findings suggest EBSS policy should emphasize multimodal integration and service reliability calibrated to EBSS’s genuine but bounded role in sustainable urban mobility.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Deployment-oriented validation of vessel energy efficiency inference for maritime decarbonisation policy
abstract: AI-based vessel fuel-consumption models are used for emission accounting, compliance screening, and decarbonisation planning, but their reported accuracy depends on how validation is designed. Using high-frequency data from 27 ocean-going vessels, this study tests whether random mixed validation overstates model performance. We compare it with maritime use-case tests for later-period prediction, unseen trips, unseen vessels, cross-type transfer, and data-scarce transfer. Across 64 model-task combinations, use-case-aligned held-out errors are 9.18 percentage points higher on average than random mixed-validation estimates. Prediction error also reverses direction across settings, indicating that accuracy metrics alone can hide policy-relevant over- or under-estimation. In a container-ship CII case study, rating accuracy ranges from 34.4% to 71.7%, while 11.7% to 100.0% of action-required D/E vessel-years are missed. These results indicate that regulatory and planning applications require validation aligned with the intended maritime use case, with reporting of both error magnitude and bias direction.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Explaining COVID-19 Tokyo metro station-level ridership disruption and recovery: pre-pandemic demand, built environment and centrality
abstract: COVID-19 caused severe and uneven metro ridership declines. This study examines station-level annual ridership change in Tokyo from 2020 to 2023 relative to 2019, integrating pre-pandemic demand, built environment, and network centrality. Its main contribution is to identify how these factors shaped ridership resilience from acute disruption to recovery using ordinary least squares (OLS) and geographically weighted regression (GWR). Results show that high pre-pandemic demand and Production and Service intensity are associated with larger proportional losses, especially in 2020–2021. Road density is consistently linked to smaller declines and stronger recovery, indicating the importance of local access networks. Land-use mix becomes increasingly positive during recovery, suggesting that functionally diverse station areas better supported localized daily activities. Destination accessibility and centrality show more spatially uneven and temporally unstable effects. These findings suggest that resilience-oriented planning should combine targeted operations for vulnerable high-demand stations with local access improvements and mixed-use station-area development.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Sustainable cold recycled pavements: performance, leaching behavior, and life cycle assessment
abstract: Sustainable transportation demands resilient infrastructure. While cold in-place recycling (CIR) lowers emissions, moisture susceptibility compromises long-term durability. Existing research rarely integrates micro-scale thermodynamics of alternative fillers with macro-scale lifecycle environmental assessments. To bridge this gap, this study evaluates the thermodynamic, mechanical, and environmental performance of CIR mixtures incorporating steel slag (SS) and rice husk ash (RHA) using surface free energy (SFE), dynamic modulus, contaminant leaching, and life cycle assessment (LCA). Results indicate optimal substitutions (75% SS and 50% RHA) provide favorable multi-scale improvements. For SS-75, SFE increased by 49%, yielding a suitable moisture resistance with a Tensile Strength Ratio (TSR) of 88.97%, while dynamic modulus improved. This structural enhancement permits thinner virgin asphalt overlays, ensuring safe contaminant encapsulation. Consequently, SS-75 reduced global warming potential by 15.2%, energy demand by 16.6%, acidification by 16.2%, and ozone depletion by 12.8%. These findings offer generalizable evidence for environmentally optimized pavement management.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Urban transportation, environment, and community health for New York City (UTECH-NYC)
abstract: Urban traffic remains a major source of fine particulate pollution and the related health burdens. We developed an urban transportation, environment, and community health model for NYC (UTECH-NYC), an integrated framework linking travel demand, on-road emissions, dispersion, and human exposure at 20 m × 20 m spatial and hourly temporal resolution. UTECH-NYC enables analysis of transportation policies such as congestion pricing and vehicle electrification. Results show that the NYC congestion toll reduces traffic-attributable PM2.5 by 16% and exposure by 13% in Manhattan’s central business district, while displacing pollution to peripheral corridors. Furthermore, vehicle-electrification scenarios reduce traffic-attributable PM2.5 across NYC. However, under the stylized uniform-adoption scenarios considered here, spatially uneven burdens are not fully eliminated, and the distributional implications are sensitive to the equity metric used. UTECH-NYC therefore provides a fine-scale, equity-aware framework for evaluation of urban transportation policies.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: The collaborative road clearing problem for Post-Disaster emergency response
abstract: After a disaster, the immediate response operations focus on reducing human suffering by restoring access to essential relief services, while long-term recovery emphasizes infrastructure reconstruction. This study addresses road clearing decisions in the immediate response phase, when restoring critical connectivity is crucial and conventional repair models may be inadequate. Approaches based solely on cost or speed may fail to reconnect the most critical routes for isolated communities. To address this gap, we propose the Collaborative Road Clearing Problem for Post-Disaster Emergency Response, which prioritizes reconnecting affected areas to critical infrastructure such as ports and airports. The model explicitly accounts for collaboration among multiple clearing teams, allowing joint operations on severely obstructed roads. A mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a heuristic are introduced. The numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of collaboration, particularly in large networks and scenarios with long clearance times.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Route-informed planning for medium- and heavy-duty truck charging infrastructure in California
abstract: California freight electrification depends as much on charging access and corridor planning as on vehicle adoption. Public agencies and fleets need evidence on whether depot and public charging networks can support truckload operations without increasing empty repositioning, modeled charging-stop requirements, and route infeasibility. This study develops an operations-based freight charging assessment for mixed diesel and battery-electric truck operations and applies it to controlled California truckload scenarios. Rather than optimizing final station sites, the framework evaluates predefined depot-adjacent and public fast-charging sites through route feasibility, total and deadhead VMT, modeled charging stop rows, active charging locations, and cost-accounting indicators. The results are scenario-level route-record comparisons and do not reflect observed daily truck operations or session-level charging dwell measurements.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Data-driven modelling of passenger-car stock electrification: validation and cross-country scenarios
abstract: Electrification policy targets new registrations, but the transition of the national passenger-car stock depends jointly on BEV adoption and vehicle retirement. This study models both, using the Czech Republic as an ageing-market case. A power-law registration function is calibrated on Czech data for 2016–2024 and benchmarked against five reference countries; a fixed-lifetime stock-turnover model, with an age-structured extension, then gives post-2035 trajectories. The adoption parameter α is a reduced-form capacity measure reflecting affordability, policy continuity and charging access. Adjusted MAPE is 6.1–17.2 % with R 2 above 0.92; the Czech in-sample fit gives MAPE 5.8 %, R 2 0.974, α cal 0.034 and n cal 2.81. Vehicle lifetime alone sets the nominal replacement horizon r d = r 0 + L: 2047 for L = 12 years, 2055 for L = 20, while α scn = 0.10–0.40 governs the stock trajectory, not the terminal year. Results are scenario comparisons, not forecasts.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Modeling Taxi-Metro Competition: Uncovering Nonlinear Influences of Trip and Built Environment Factors
abstract: Understanding taxi-metro competition is crucial for optimizing the modal split where both modes serve overlapping origin-destination (OD) pairs. This study examines the nonlinear factors associated with taxi-metro competition strength in Chengdu, defined as the proportion of taxi trips among the combined taxi and metro trips for each OD pair. To account for bounded competition strength, we propose a hybrid model combining Beta regression with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Beta-BART), which achieves better predictive performance than gradient-boosted decision trees and BART. The results show that OD distance has the highest relative importance (6.2%) and that competition strength declines sharply as OD distance increases to about 7.5 km, with little change beyond this distance. Furthermore, land use mix exhibits an inverted-U association, with competition strength peaking near 0.80. Practically, these nonlinear patterns can inform more targeted transport planning. Methodologically, the framework provides a template for modeling proportional transportation outcomes with bounded distributions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: To what extent do green roads generate ecological gains?
abstract: Road expansion in fragile plateau regions can cause multidimensional ecological disturbance, yet the relative performance of green-road sections remains uncertain. We assessed the Tongsai Expressway on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau using a matched-reference structure–quality–function framework integrating propensity score matching, land-cover- and distance-stratified gain analysis, and exploratory interpretable machine learning. Green-road sections showed selective rather than universal gains. Statistically supported gains were concentrated in Green Road 2, particularly woodland quality indicators (NDVI, NDBSI, WET) at 300–500 m and grassland water conservation (12.470–18.618 mm) at 100–500 m, whereas structural and composite-index gains lacked consistent support. Variation in estimated road eco-effects was associated with road distance, land cover, elevation, climate, and built-up proximity. Climate-enhanced matching and equal-primary-dimension weighting retained the main patterns. Because this is a single-corridor, non-replicated case study with section-specific spatial and temporal contexts, the findings represent case-specific associations rather than causal effects of individual green-road measures.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Calibrating fiscal policy signals for ammonia fuel adoption in shipping
abstract: Ammonia is a promising zero-carbon shipping fuel, yet uptake remains sluggish. This study calibrates budget-constrained fiscal instruments to promote shipowner adoption and sustain diffusion while ensuring supplier profitability, supply stability, and government payoff. We develop a two-layer Stackelberg model with the government as leader and shipowners and fuel suppliers as followers. In the static layer, the optimum is identified by gridding tax and subsidy; in the dynamic layer, ODEs track 100-month trajectories. Results show an interior optimum within the fiscal corridor at 99,79, delivering 99.996 % static adoption, an equilibrium price of USD1,080/t, and about 87.06 % penetration. Dynamics converge stably, with learning-driven price declines and rising composite government utility. The optimum serves as a policy anchor: maintain the carbon tax as a long-run signal and front-load then phase down the subsidy as adoption increases. Within the corridor, fiscal parameters are adaptively adjusted to observed adoption, profitability, and net fiscal burden.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Heterogeneous bus ridership responses to micro-scale built environment: Evidence from explainable AI
abstract: Despite the inherent complexity of urban mobility, conventional methodologies often oversimplify the associations between transit demand and built environment, leaving nonlinearity and behavioral asymmetries obscured. This study integrates computer vision and explainable artificial intelligence (XGBoost-SHAP) to decode how the micro-scale built environment affects multidimensional bus ridership. Six environmental visual proxies were extracted through semantic segmentation from 3,736 street view imagery, and subsequently analyzed alongside 8.6 million ridership records over one month across 934 bus stops in Shenzhen, China. Four models distinguish temporal-behavioral patterns (weekday peak vs. weekend off-peak, boarding vs. alighting). The results reveal behavioral heterogeneity: stronger correlations were observed in boarding than alighting demand, while weekend discretionary trips exhibit greater sensitivity to micro-environmental quality than weekday mandatory trips. By quantifying nonlinear threshold effects and diminishing marginal utilities, this study develops a spatial screening matrix that supports planners in flagging environmental mismatches and advancing transit-demand-oriented, data-driven transportation planning.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: An option-insurance hedging framework for EU ETS maritime compliance costs
abstract: The inclusion of the maritime sector in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) exposes shipowners to dual compliance risks: carbon price volatility and unexpected excess emissions from emission-reduction equipment failures. We propose a novel risk management framework integrating an EUA Price Call Option (EPCO) and a Carbon Emission Equipment Loss Insurance (CEELI). We develop a rigorous pricing model that incorporates the joint stochastic dynamics of carbon prices and EUR/USD exchange rates, alongside the “bathtub” reliability curve of abatement technologies. A case study demonstrates that the framework successfully translates operational risks into transparent, budgetable upfront premiums, providing a “cost of certainty” for operators. Furthermore, scenario analyses reveal a dynamic operational-financial interaction mechanism: EPCO adoption is driven by EEA voyage exposure and cost pass-through capacity, whereas CEELI acts as a strategic financial enabler for fleet retrofitting. We provide a highly adaptable financial toolkit for shipping operators navigating the EU ETS transition.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Environmental operating points in the AV era: beyond capacity maximization
abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) can increase network capacity, but capacity-oriented control may keep urban traffic near instability-prone states and intensify environmental burdens. This paper develops a macroscopic framework for identifying an operating point that minimizes environmentally augmented social cost (EASC) in AV-era networks. The framework represents urban traffic network operating conditions using an MFD-based formulation, combines jam-state travel-time reliability risk with a link-speed-volatility proxy for stop-and-go emissions, and validates the baseline volatility proxy against CAPSS-based emission estimates. AV penetration, effective response delay, and routing coordination are modeled as macroscopic levers reshaping capacity, jam prevalence, and dynamic burdens. Under AV scenarios in Seoul calibrated using human-driven traffic, the EASC-minimizing operating point can lie below the conventional MFD capacity density, suggesting that maximum throughput is not necessarily environmentally desirable. Sustainable AV control may therefore need to prioritize reductions in jam-state risk, travel-time unreliability, and speed-volatility-induced emissions rather than capacity maximization alone.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Multi-source data fusion for ship carbon emission prediction with language-model decision support
abstract: International maritime transport contributes 2.89% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) and European Union (EU) rules increasingly require voyage-level prediction with auditable guidance. This study proposes Maritime-FTNet, a multi-source fusion model encoding Automatic Identification System (AIS) kinematics, meteorological reanalysis and vessel static parameters through vessel-conditioned feature selection, gated temporal-channel attention and Mixup regularisation. On 18 months of US-coastal container-shipping data, it attains a coefficient of determination of R2=0.7529±0.0066 for next-day prediction over ten seeds and outperforms ten 10-seed baselines spanning tree-based, recurrent and Transformer families (all p < 0.01 with bootstrap intervals); at multi-day horizons a gradient-boosting baseline becomes competitive. An optional tool-augmented language-model layer grounded in six engineering tools and self-verification delivers emission attribution, Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) compliance assessment and speed recommendations. Built on public input sources, the framework supports IMO and EU compliance monitoring.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Spatial variations of non-exhaust emissions across seasons using fixed-site and mobile measurements
abstract: Urban exposure to particulate matter (PM) from road dust and brake and tire wear (BTW) is an emerging health concern. Mobile and fixed-site PM sampling was conducted seasonally in Toronto. Mobile sampling employed paired window and wheel-well inlets to estimate resuspended PM, alongside ultrafine particles and black carbon as indicators of exhaust emissions. Analysis of 900+ weekly filters from 40 sites showed the strongest roadway contrasts for barium. Source apportionment resolved distinct contributions from road dust and BTW. Road dust dominated the trace element mass in PM, peaking in construction areas, while BTW contributed 10–15 % and peaked near expressways. Mobile measurements revealed steep near-road ultrafine particle gradients and increased resuspended PM on local roads, particularly in winter. However, non-exhaust emission rates remained greatest on expressways. This study presents the first integration of fixed-site and mobile measurements with spatial source apportionment and land use regression with kriging to characterize non-exhaust emissions.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Dynamic collaborative optimization of wind-assisted ship energy efficiency under variable navigational conditions
abstract: Ship energy efficiency (SEE) optimization is an effective method to promote energy conservation and emission reduction for the shipping industry. Existing optimization techniques are limited to single-dimensional optimization of sailing route or speed, lacking a comprehensive approach that can achieve dynamic and synergistic optimization of ship energy efficiency, especially for wind-assisted ships. Therefore, a dynamic collaborative optimization method for the wind-assisted ship energy efficiency is proposed in this paper. The coupling effects among sailing speed, sail’s angle of attack (AOA), and various environmental variables are integrated into a unified framework to achieve the dynamic SEE optimization. The case study demonstrates that the proposed dynamic collaborative optimization method can reduce fuel consumption by 4.03 %. Compared with static optimization method, the optimization effects can be further improved by 1.19 %. The proposed method is of great significance for further improving the wind-assisted ship energy efficiency, thus promoting the shipping decarbonization.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Road contexts shape spatial patterns of bat assemblages in tropical dry forests
abstract: Road infrastructure can shape biodiversity patterns, yet evidence from tropical systems remains limited. We assessed variation in bat assemblages across four road contexts (Old, Operational, Under Construction, Mitigation area) and three distances from the road edge (0, 300, 2000 m) in a Colombian tropical dry forest. Assemblages were sampled using mist nets and passive acoustic monitoring and integrated as operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Taxonomic diversity and composition varied among road contexts and sampled distances. After standardization to a common sample coverage, Hill diversity was higher at the sampled 2000 m distance than at 0 m in the Under Construction and Operational contexts, whereas the Mitigation area and Old context showed different spatial patterns. Beta-diversity analyses showed that compositional differentiation among sampled distances involved both taxonomic-unit turnover and nestedness, with the relative contribution of these components varying among road contexts. Guild representation also varied among contexts and distances, with aerial insectivores predominating in most context × distance combinations. Because environmental drivers were not directly measured and each context corresponds to a single site, these results are descriptive rather than tests of causal road effects. These findings reveal context-dependent spatial variation in bat assemblages across the sampled distances and provide a descriptive baseline for designing future studies that explicitly evaluate the mechanisms and spatial extent of road-associated effects.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Perceived neighbourhood environments, social trust, and intentions to purchase alternative fuel vehicles
abstract: Despite advances in transport technology, ownership of alternative fuel vehicles (AFVs) remains markedly lower than that of conventional vehicles. While prior work has highlighted the influence of the built environment on AFV ownership, the social mechanisms underlying this relationship are less well understood, particularly the mediating role of social trust. This study investigates the direct and indirect associations between the perceived neighbourhood environment and intention to purchase AFVs, with trust in public institutions and neighbours as mediators. Our findings show that neighbourhoods characterised by good physical activity infrastructure, greater accessibility, and perceived safety are associated with higher levels of trust in public institutions, which in turn increases individuals’ intention to purchase AFVs. The results emphasise the relevance of land-use policies for promoting environmentally sustainable cities and underscore the modest but significant role of social mechanisms in linking land-use policy to AFV ownership.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Social influences on the adoption of electric vehicles: A meta-analysis
abstract: This study conducts a meta‑analysis of 152 primary estimates to examine how social influences affect electric vehicle (EV) adoption. We distinguish between informational influences (social interaction and neighborhood effect) and normative influences (social norm and social symbolism). The results confirm a significant overall effect of social influences on EV adoption, with normative influences outweighing informational ones. Over time, the dominant normative driver shifts from social symbolism to social norm. Cross‑sectionally, social norm is more influential in collectivistic cultures and for conservative innovations, whereas informational social interaction is more influential in individualistic cultures and for radical innovations. Based on these findings, we recommend celebrity endorsements to amplify social symbolism in early market stages, and green labelling to reinforce social norm in mature markets. Community-based campaigns that foster social interaction are suggested for individualistic regions and radical innovations, while broad publicity emphasizing social norm is suggested for collectivistic regions and conservative innovations.

title: Housing type mix as a lever for sustainable urban mobility
abstract: Land use-transport interactions are well documented in literature using urban form metrics including density, land–use mix, and destination accessibility, but rarely housing type shares. This study demonstrates the overlooked explanatory and causal relevance of housing typology, specifically the single–family housing share, for four mobility outcomes: car travel, transit travel, car ownership, and CO 2 emissions. Using postcode–level data for 13 cities in Germany and France, we compare the role of urban form metrics across linear regression, gradient–boosted decision trees, artificial neural networks, causal discovery, and double machine learning methods. Single–family share consistently outperforms conventional urban form indicators in explaining each outcome. Given its strong predictive power, causal relevance, and ease of measurement, housing typology offers substantial potential for modelling land use-transport interactions and provides a promising cross–sectoral focus for climate and mobility policy.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Environmental impacts of bidirectional charging for electric school buses: a cross-regional assessment
abstract: Electric school buses can interact bidirectionally with the grid during overnight idle periods, but their environmental consequences are poorly understood. This study develops a multi-objective overnight scheduling framework for electric school bus fleets that jointly optimizes charging costs, grid export, and age-dependent battery degradation under discrete charger-assignment constraints. A cross-regional assessment across six US grid subregions shows the net CO2 effect is region-dependent, yielding reductions where the peak-to-off-peak marginal emission factor ratio is high and increases where it is low; coal-dominated grids produce net increases under current generation mixes. Benchmarking against smart unidirectional charging isolates what export itself contributes: deeper CO2 and NOx reductions, but higher SO2 and a reversal of the PM2.5 benefit that unidirectional charging delivers. These outcomes are robust across five fleet scales, six utility tariffs, and five climate zones, though their magnitude depends on regional grid composition, arguing against blanket environmental credits and in favor of region-specific policy design.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Effects of station-area built environment on urban rail transit passenger flow
abstract: Global urban rail transit (URT) faces operational inefficiencies due to spatiotemporal mismatches between stations and urban functions. Existing research overemphasizes average daily ridership, lacking insights into built environment effects’ variations by station type, time and spatial scale. This study develops an integrated framework of station classification and multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) to explore built environment-passenger flow mechanisms, with Changsha as a case. K-Means clustering categorizes stations into residential, employment and mixed-use types, and MGWR is compared with OLS and GWR models. Key findings: built environment impacts show distinct spatiotemporal heterogeneity, functional-type dependence and scale variability; educational/cultural facilities and entrance/exit numbers steadily drive passenger flow; office density has divergent effects across station types and peak/off-peak periods. The framework identifies variables’ operational scales, offering a refined analytical tool for spatial patterns, deepening station-city dynamic theories and enabling tailored URT planning governance.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Exploring future sustainable urban transport through scenarios: a critical review of contemporary practice
abstract: Under deep uncertainty, long-range transport forecasts are prone to inaccuracy. Scenario planning – a foresight approach from futures studies – offers a means to explore different long-range transport possibilities while also engaging transport stakeholders. Transport scenario narratives constitute a rich dataset of qualitative insights to draw upon concerning contemporary transport foresight. In this paper, thematic analysis and synthesis were utilised both to identify key ideas being explored through transport scenario planning and to evaluate sampled published transport scenario narratives critically. Through standardized keyword queries of Google Scholar, published documentation from 40 scenario planning projects were identified that met the study criteria. Sampled published transport scenario narratives (n = 173) from 40 scenario planning projects, across 25 countries, were analysed; 95% of projects were published in peer-reviewed academic journals. This study’s results provide a thematic map exploring the principal concerns captured by sampled published transport scenario narratives and opportunities for improvement are discussed as a set of recommendations for enhancing transport scenario narrative quality.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Balancing sustainability and employer attractiveness: strategy–structure alignment in corporate mobility management
abstract: Commuting and business travel significantly contribute to transport emissions, requiring companies to reduce their environmental impact. Simultaneously, mobility benefits have become an important factor in employer attractiveness. Corporate mobility management is therefore gaining relevance for organizations, aiming for sustainable and attractive concepts. This study examines strategic drivers, organizational structures, and their relationship in corporate mobility management. The analysis draws on an exploratory case study of seven employers, using multiple data sources. First, the results show that organizations often perceive tensions between sustainability and employer attractiveness, as key drivers of new mobility initiatives. Second, the structure of corporate mobility management ranges from dedicated to distributed roles. Lastly, the primary driver of an initiative is typically reflected in the department leading it. This study thereby conceptualizes corporate mobility management as a peripheral, cross-functional organizational domain in which strategy–structure alignment emerges through parallel and overlapping arrangements shaped by multiple strategic drivers.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Do low emission zones generate car fleet renewal? A quasi-natural experiment
abstract: This study evaluates whether the introduction of Low Emission Zones accelerates car fleet renewal. To achieve this aim, this study uses the 2017 introduction of the Ultra Low Emission Zone in London, United Kingdom. This policy required drivers of older cars (Euro 4 or older) to pay a £10 charge per day to enter a specific area of central London. A spatial difference-in-differences empirical design is implemented to estimate the causal impact of the policy. Findings of the analysis are that the introduction of this policy increased vehicle fleet renewal by 2.2%. A practical use of this finding is that such ancillary benefits can now be included in the business case development for such policies, quantifying the broader spectrum of positive outcomes that can be realised.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Commuting matters: Association between work travel and perceived health and well-being in Canada
abstract: Beyond its functional role, commuting can have far-reaching consequences on the health and well-being of workers. This study examines the relationship between commute mode choice and physical health (PH), mental health (MH), and life in general (LiG) using data from the Canadian Mobility Survey (N = 6,671). We estimate weighted logistic regression models, accounting for commute duration, reasons for mode choice, sociodemographic characteristics, and concurrent life and health satisfaction. Results show that cycling and walking to work were associated with better PH, MH, and LiG than driving. Rapid transit users reported better PH, while bus commuters had lower odds for LiG than drivers. Overall, the findings highlight that commuting experiences are linked to multiple dimensions of well-being. Policies that prioritize active commuting and improve the quality and accessibility of public transit may contribute to better physical, mental, and overall well-being of commuters.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: High-Speed rail expansion and avian Biodiversity Decline: Evidence from a Hub-Link Perspective
abstract: Although the economic effects of high-speed rail (HSR) are well documented, its implications for avian biodiversity remain unclear. Using a county-level panel for China from 2002 to 2020, we combine effort-adjusted indices from citizen science bird records with geospatial data on HSR lines and stations and estimate treatment effects using a Double Machine Learning (DML) framework. A hub-link decomposition indicates that the negative estimate for avian biodiversity is concentrated in counties with HSR stations, whereas pass-through corridors have no detectable average effect at the county scale. The mechanism analysis is consistent with increased human activity and land conversion around stations. A micro-spatial buffer analysis further shows that the avian estimates are most negative within 1 km of stations and diminish with distance. These findings suggest that ecological assessments of HSR projects should consider not only rail alignments but also station-area land development.

title: Dynamic decarbonization pathways for inland shipping under energy system and policy uncertainties
abstract: Inland shipping decarbonization requires coordinated changes in fleets, fuels, infrastructure, and policy that static life cycle assessments cannot capture. This study develops a framework coupling Power-to-X pathways, dynamic hybrid life cycle assessment, a fleet digital twin, and multi-objective optimization. Applied to 2,100 weighted representative vessel records in the Yangtze River Delta from 2025 to 2050 under four policy scenarios, the selected integrated policy knee solution reduces diesel from 99.0% to 15.5% of fleet shaft energy demand. Battery electricity becomes the largest low-carbon pathway (30.3%), followed by hydrogen (22.1%), e-methanol (16.4%), and ammonia (15.6%). Cumulative life cycle emissions are 298.8 Mt CO2-eq, 10.4% below business as usual, while net present resource cost is 166.3 billion 2025 USD. Deep inland shipping decarbonization is feasible but back-loaded and depends on coordinated fleet renewal, infrastructure deployment, and fuel diversification.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Reducing carbon emission by optimizing container liner fleet deployment and sailing speed
abstract: Facing stringent environmental regulations and an aging fleet, container liner shipping companies face mounting pressure to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This paper optimizes tactical fleet deployment and sailing speed by explicitly incorporating vessel heterogeneity. A mixed integer nonlinear programming model is formulated, and a Velocity-Discretization-Based Dynamic Algorithm is developed to improve computational efficiency. Practical fleet adjustment constraints are further considered to evaluate the achievable benefits under limited vessel redeployment. Numerical experiments based on real-world operational data demonstrate that considering vessel heterogeneity and jointly optimizing deployment and speed can significantly reduce fuel consumption and CO2 emissions. The proposed algorithm achieves reliable solutions with substantially shorter computational time than the direct solution, providing a practical decision-support tool for sustainable liner shipping operations.
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Environmental impacts of development of railways in a road dominated infrastructure
abstract: Railway infrastructure plays a pivotal role in economic development, with well-documented environmental implications. However, emerging global agreements, climate change, and evolving environmental policies introduce new dimensions that must be considered. The expansion of Brazil's railway network has the potential to transform landscapes. This study evaluates the environmental impacts of railway expansion, focusing on land cover changes driven by proximity to infrastructure, population density, and agricultural potential. Spatial analysis and Random Forest modelling reveal significant risks of natural area conversion, with notable overlap between predicted impacts and ecologically sensitive regions such as Key Biodiversity Areas, protected areas, and threatened species. While scenario-specific analyses highlight variations in potential impacts, the primary finding is clear: railways function as major drivers of landscape transformation, amplifying anthropogenic pressures on natural habitats. These results underscore the urgent need for proactive conservation planning to mitigate ecological impacts and ensure that infrastructure development aligns with global biodiversity goals
journal_title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

title: Carbon mitigation potential of metro-based underground urban logistics under operational constraints
abstract: Rising urban freight and decarbonization pressures raise an increasingly pressing question: can metros provide green freight mobility without harming passengers? We develop a policy-evaluation framework for metro-based underground logistics (MUL) that integrates multi-task demand forecasting, capacity-constrained freight realization, and emissions accounting under passenger-priority operations. Shanghai's empirical results have showed that freight demand peaks tend to occur outside passenger peaks, while high-volume freight OD flows are less concentrated along major passenger commuting corridors. Under our baseline setting, MUL realizes 66.69% of metro-replaceable demand on weekdays and 92.28% on weekends, with estimated net CO2 reductions of 14.86% and 24.32%, respectively, after accounting for feeder travel, detours, and unrealized demand. The weekend estimate is more sensitive to freight-demand prediction uncertainty. Scenario comparisons identify station-proximate eligibility, direct routing, off-peak operation, and freight capacity allocation as the main operational levers shaping mitigation.
